bib.title: Unsupervised Dense Information Retrieval with Contrastive Learning

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Unsupervised Dense Information Retrieval with Contrastive Learning", Gautier Izacard, Mathilde Caron, Lucas Hosseini, Sebastian Riedel, Piotr Bojanowski, Armand Joulin, Edouard Grave (Meta AI Research et al.). Transactions on Machine Learning Research (08/2022); arXiv:2112.09118v4, 29 Aug 2022.
PDF: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/02-rag-retrieval/sources/izacard-2021-unsupervised-dense-information-retrieval-contrastive.pdf

COVERAGE: I read all 75,168 of 75,168 chars, pages 1–21. That covers the body, the ablations, the discussion, Appendix A (A.1–A.3, Table 10) and Appendix B (B.1–B.3, Tables 11–15). I skimmed the references for origins only. I did not run figures.py: both figure captions came through cleanly in the text.

CLAIMS
- claim: With no labelled data, Contriever beats BM25 on 11 of 15 BEIR datasets at Recall@100. Its average Recall@100 is still below BM25's.
  number: 11/15. Average Recall@100 is 60.1 for Contriever and 63.6 for BM25.
  setup: Unsupervised, BERT-base, BEIR test sets. Trec-COVID uses capped recall. BM25 is 3 points better on average because it wins Trec-COVID (49.8 vs 17.2) and Touche (53.8 vs 22.5) by wide margins.
  quote: "it obtains better performance than BM25 on 11 out of 15 datasets from the benchmark for the recall@100" / Table 11 row "Avg. 63.6 19.0 45.4 46.9 60.1"
  where: p.7 §4.3; p.19 Table 11. I recounted Table 11 myself and got 11/15. Table 11's "Best on" row gives Contriever 10 because that count includes the other baselines.
- claim: At nDCG@10, the unsupervised model still loses to BM25. BM25 is best on 12 of 15 datasets.
  number: Average nDCG@10 is 36.0 for Contriever and 41.7 for BM25. Best-on counts are 12 for BM25 and 2 for Contriever.
  setup: Same unsupervised setting. The authors blame Trec-COVID (the training data predates COVID) and Touche-2020 (long documents).
  quote: "while Contriever largely closes the gap between unsupervised retrievers and BM25, it is still outperformed by BM25 as reported in Table 11" / Table 11 nDCG rows "Avg. 41.7 8.7 24.6 25.1 36.0" and "Best on 12 0 1 0 2"
  where: p.7; p.19
- claim: The authors make Recall@100 their main metric, although nDCG@10 is BEIR's main metric. Their reason is that a downstream reader or re-ranker consumes the top 100.
  number: none
  setup: Their own framing.
  quote: "While nDCG@10 is the main metric of BEIR, we are more interested in the Recall@100 to evaluate bi-encoders, as our goal is to develop retrievers that can be used in ML systems."
  where: p.6 §4.1
- claim: Positive pairs come from independent random cropping, meaning two spans sampled from the same document, with 10% token deletion. This beat ICT in the ablation.
  number: nDCG@10 overall is 25.9 for ICT, 32.2 for crop, 33.8 for crop + delete and 32.9 for crop + replace.
  setup: Unsupervised, Wikipedia only, 200k steps, batch size 2,048, 7 BEIR datasets.
  quote: "ICT 23.2 19.4 31.6 27.6 21.3 10.6 55.6 25.9 / Crop 27.6 ... 32.2 / Crop + delete ... 33.8"
  where: p.13 Table 7. The authors' reason (p.4): "Independent cropping also lead to overlap between the two views of the data, hence encouraging the network to learn exact matches between the query and document, in a way that is similar to lexical matching methods like BM25". They also say the symmetric query and key distributions make MoCo training more stable (p.12).
- claim: In the final recipe, documents are 256 tokens and span lengths are 5–50% of the document. Training uses MoCo with a queue of 131,072, momentum 0.9995 and temperature 0.05, with batch size 2,048 for 500k steps on 50/50 Wikipedia/CCNet.
  number: queue 131,072; momentum 0.9995; τ 0.05
  setup: English Contriever, initialised from BERT base uncased, AdamW, learning rate 5e-5.
  quote: "we use the MoCo algorithm He et al. (2020) with a queue of size 131,072, a momentum value of 0.9995 and a temperature of 0.05. We use the random cropping data augmentation, with documents of 256 tokens and span sizes sampled between 5% and 50% of the document length."
  where: p.17 App. A.1
- claim: With the number of negatives held equal, MoCo did not beat in-batch negatives (in-batch scored slightly higher unsupervised). The authors chose MoCo because its queue scales without a larger batch.
  number: average nDCG@10 is 30.1 for MoCo and 31.9 for in-batch negatives.
  setup: Batch size 4,096 with the queue capped at 4,096, unsupervised, 8 BEIR datasets.
  quote: "MoCo 26.2 13.1 13.7 33.0 69.5 20.0 11.9 57.6 30.1 / In-batch negatives 24.2 21.6 13.0 33.7 74.9 17.9 13.6 56.1 31.9"; "We thus propose to use MoCo as our contrastive learning framework, since it scales to a larger number of negative examples without the need to increase the batch size."
  where: p.11 Table 6 and text
- claim: More negatives help on average across BEIR, mostly in the unsupervised setting, and not equally on every dataset.
  number: queue sizes from 2,048 to 131,072
  setup: Figure 2, nDCG@10 with and without MS MARCO fine-tuning.
  quote: "We consider values ranging from 2,048 to 131,072 ... increasing the number of negatives leads to better retrieval performance, especially in the unsupervised setting. However, we note that this effect is not equally strong for all datasets."
  where: p.11
- claim: After MS MARCO fine-tuning, Contriever has the best average nDCG@10 among the bi-encoders shown, below the sparse Splade v2. It is state of the art on Recall@100. Re-ranking its results with a cross-encoder gives state-of-the-art average nDCG@10.
  number: Average nDCG@10 without CQA is 47.5, against 50.6 for Splade v2, 43.7 for TAS-B and 44.0 for BM25. Ours+CE reaches 51.2. Recall@100 rises from 65.0 to 67.1, and Ours+CE is "Best on" 9 datasets.
  setup: 14 BEIR datasets (3 excluded for licence), MS MARCO excluded from the average. Re-ranker: ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2. Fine-tuning used ASAM, in-batch negatives and one round of hard-negative mining, with no distillation.
  quote: "contriever obtains the best results among dense bi-encoder methods for the nDCG@10, and is state-of-the-art for the recall@100 (improving the average recall@100 from 65.0 to 67.1)"; Table 2 "Avg. w/o CQA 44.0 49.5 26.3 41.3 43.7 43.1 45.1 50.6 47.5 51.2"
  where: p.8 Table 2 and text; p.18 Table 10
- claim: Most of the fine-tuned gain comes from the pre-training. When BERT gets the same fine-tuning, it scores lower.
  number: nDCG@10 overall is 42.0 for BERT and 46.5 for Contriever.
  setup: Ablation-scale models, MS MARCO fine-tuning for 20k steps, 8 BEIR datasets.
  quote: "BERT 28.2 44.6 25.9 35.0 84.0 34.4 13.0 69.8 42.0 / Contriever 33.2 50.2 28.8 46.0 85.4 38.8 16.0 77.7 46.5"
  where: p.13 Table 9
- claim: In the few-shot setting, pre-training alone beats BERT even when BERT is first fine-tuned on MS MARCO.
  number: SciFact nDCG@10 is 84.0 for Contriever, 80.9 for BERT+MS MARCO and 66.5 for BM25. FiQA is 36.4 against 30.9.
  setup: 729, 2,590 and 5,500 in-domain training queries; 500 epochs.
  quote: "Contriever - 84.0 33.6 36.4 / BERT ms marco 80.9 33.2 30.9"
  where: p.8 Table 3
- claim: On unsupervised open-domain QA, Contriever beats BM25 on NQ at R@100 and ties it on TriviaQA.
  number: NQ R@100 is 82.1 against 78.3. TriviaQA R@100 is 83.2 against 83.2.
  setup: Wikipedia Dec-2018 dump.
  quote: "BM25 (Ma et al., 2021) - 62.9 78.3 - 76.4 83.2 / Contriever 47.8 67.8 82.1 59.4 74.2 83.2"
  where: p.7 Table 1
- claim: On Mr. TyDi (monolingual, 11 languages), unsupervised mContriever beats BM25 on average Recall@100 but trails it on MRR@100. After MS MARCO fine-tuning it is state of the art on R@100.
  number: average R@100 is 77.2 for mContriever and 74.3 for BM25. Average MRR@100 is 25.0 against 33.3. With MS MARCO, R@100 is 87.0, and adding Mr. TyDi fine-tuning gives 93.6.
  setup: mBERT init, 29 pre-training languages, queue 32,768.
  quote: Table 4 rows "BM25 ... 33.3", "mContriever ... 25.0", "BM25 ... 74.3", "mContriever ... 77.2", "+ MS MARCO ... 87.0"
  where: p.10 Table 4
- claim: For cross-lingual retrieval (queries in 26 languages against English Wikipedia), fine-tuning on English-only MS MARCO beats CORA. Unsupervised mContriever is well below CORA.
  number: average R@100 is 65.6 for mContriever+MS MARCO, 59.8 for CORA and 49.2 for unsupervised mContriever.
  setup: Derived from MKQA, 6,619 queries, lowercased.
  quote: "CORA (Asai et al., 2021) 49.0 59.8 ... / mContriever 31.4 49.2 ... / + MS MARCO 53.9 65.6"
  where: p.11 Table 5
- claim: Adding pre-training languages hurts quality ("curse of multilinguality").
  number: Mr. TyDi average R@100 is 78.9 with 11 languages and 77.2 with 29.
  quote: "11 languages 83.4 ... 78.9 / 29 languages 82.0 ... 77.2"
  where: p.21 Table 15

LIMITS: The authors concede that the unsupervised model is "competitive with BM25 (albeit not state-of-the-art)" (p.13). It still loses to BM25 on nDCG@10, on average Recall@100, on Trec-COVID, on Touche-2020 (long documents) and on Mr. TyDi MRR@100. Their MS MARCO fine-tuning is deliberately simple, with no distillation, so it is not compared against stronger recipes on equal terms. Three BEIR datasets are excluded for licence reasons. All ablations use the small Wikipedia-only setting. Every model is BERT-base. The paper reports no latency, no index size and no comparison with hybrid BM25+dense (except Mr. TyDi's reported Hybrid baseline, which beats unsupervised mContriever: average R@100 80.9). The temperature for multilingual pre-training was not tuned. On dating: these baselines are from 2021, and later embedders such as E5, GTE and BGE are absent, so "state of the art" is stale.

BUILDS ON: InfoNCE/instance discrimination (Wu et al., 2018); MoCo (He et al., 2020); SimCLR (Chen et al., 2020); ICT (Lee et al., 2019); the bi-encoder from DSSM (Huang et al., 2013) and DPR (Karpukhin et al., 2020); ANCE (Xiong et al., 2020); BEIR (Thakur et al., 2021); CCNet (Wenzek et al., 2020); BERT (Devlin et al., 2019). Concurrent work: coCondenser (Gao & Callan, 2021) and Spider (Ram et al., 2021).

CODE: none in the paper. The repo it points to is https://github.com/facebookresearch/contriever (p.2). Two equations are worth keeping, from p.4 and p.6: InfoNCE "L(q,k+) = −exp(s(q,k+)/τ) / (exp(s(q,k+)/τ) + Σ exp(s(q,ki)/τ))" and the momentum update "θk←mθk + (1−m)θq". The PDF extraction drops the log in InfoNCE, which is presumably −log of that ratio, so check the equation against the PDF before quoting it.

FIGURES:
- Fig. 1, p.5: "Unsupervised retrieval. We compare our pre-training without using any annotated data to REALM, SimCSE and BM25 ... on par with BM25 but on 2 datasets." This per-dataset Recall@100 bar chart shows the gap closing, and the two Trec-COVID/Touche outliers, at a glance.
- Fig. 2, p.12: "Impact of the number of negatives. ... nDCG@10 as a function of the queue size, with and without fine-tuning on MS MARCO." It shows uneven scaling across datasets faster than a table would.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions. Small faults:
- The InfoNCE equation lost its log and fraction layout in extraction.
- Table 2 has the stray value "37.0." for BM25+CE on CQADupStack.
- The Table 12 checkmarks did not extract, so per-language pre-training/evaluation membership is unreadable.
- Table 11 gives BM25 average nDCG@10 as 41.7 and Table 2 gives 43.0. The two use different averaging sets: Table 11 appears to include MS MARCO. Cite each average with its own table.
- Figure 1's caption ("on par ... but on 2 datasets") and the text's "11 out of 15" describe different things. Being "competitive" is not the same as winning.
